title: International Shoe Co. v. Washington (1945)
summary: Washington could enforce an employment-related contribution obligation arising from the company’s continuous in-state sales activity.
notes:
The opinion supplies the starting framework. Later cases in the course specify purposeful availment, claim relatedness, general jurisdiction, and independent routes such as consent. Its historical examples should be read alongside those later decisions.

Chief Justice Stone wrote for the Court (Justice Jackson took no part); the case is the source of the 'minimum contacts' test, and Black's separate opinion warned that the 'fair play' and 'substantial justice' criteria invite the Court to strike down state laws on its own notions of natural justice.

sections.Parties: Washington sought unpaid contributions to its unemployment-compensation system. International Shoe, incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business in St. Louis, challenged the assessment and jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts: During the relevant years the company employed approximately eleven to thirteen salesmen who lived and worked in Washington. They solicited orders, displayed samples, and sometimes rented rooms for that purpose at company expense. Orders required acceptance outside Washington; the goods were shipped from outside the state. The company had no local office or stock of merchandise and the salesmen did not make binding contracts for it. Nevertheless, their regular activities generated a continuous and substantial stream of business. The obligation being enforced arose from employing those workers in Washington.
sections.Procedural History: Washington served a notice of assessment on a local salesman and sent a copy by registered mail to the company’s home office. The company made a special appearance and challenged jurisdiction and the assessment. An administrative appeal tribunal, the commissioner, the state superior court, and the Washington Supreme Court sustained the assessment. The Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Issue: Could Washington require this out-of-state corporation to defend a proceeding to collect contributions arising from its in-state employees, consistently with due process?
sections.Holding: Yes. The company’s contacts with Washington made the particular proceeding consistent with traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice. The method of notice was also adequate in the circumstances.
sections.Reasoning: The Court treated corporate “presence” as a conclusion requiring explanation through actual activities. The decisive considerations were the quality and nature of the local operations and their connection to the obligation. Continuous solicitation by resident employees brought the company the benefits of Washington’s market and legal protections. The state’s demand concerned an obligation generated by that very employment. The company’s absence of an office, inventory, and local contracting authority therefore did not control. The opinion contrasts isolated or unrelated activity with sustained operations and explains why the relationship between contacts and suit matters; it does not give a numerical contact threshold. The local employee’s role and the mailed copy also made notice reasonably suited to communicating the proceeding.

learning.why: Washington could enforce an employment-related contribution obligation arising from the company’s continuous in-state sales activity.

topics.minimum-contacts: International Shoe formulates the due-process inquiry in terms of the quality and nature of the defendant’s forum contacts.
topics.purposeful-availment: Continuous local solicitation obtained the benefits and protection of Washington law.
topics.relatedness: The assessed unemployment contributions arose from the local employment that supplied the contacts.
topics.fairness: The relationship between activities, obligation, and forum made the proceeding fair.
topics.cp-service: Service on a local salesman, supplemented by registered mail, gave reasonable notice in this setting.
topics.cp-personal-jurisdiction: International Shoe is the foundational modern personal-jurisdiction case and belongs on the top-level concept.
topics.cp-territorial: The opinion replaced Pennoyer's presence-and-power framework with minimum contacts, so it is the pivot point in the territorial-authority narrative.
topics.general-jurisdiction: Stone's dicta on 'continuous and systematic' activities supporting suits on unrelated claims is the origin of general jurisdiction.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Black agreed with the result but criticized the majority’s open-ended fairness language. He emphasized the state’s power to regulate and adjudicate obligations generated by business conducted within its territory.

sections.Parties: International Shoe challenged Washington’s assessment of unemployment-compensation contributions.
sections.Material Facts: The company employed resident salesmen who regularly solicited orders in Washington. Orders were accepted outside the state; the assessed obligation arose from the in-state employment.
sections.Procedural History: An administrative appeal tribunal rejected the company’s special-appearance challenge. The commissioner, state superior court, and Washington Supreme Court upheld the assessment. The U.S. Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Issue: Could Washington exercise jurisdiction to enforce an obligation arising from these activities consistently with due process?
sections.Holding: Yes. The company had sufficient contacts to make this proceeding consistent with fair play and substantial justice.
sections.Reasoning: The Court examined the quality and nature of the forum activities and their relationship to the obligation. The company continuously obtained the benefits and protection of Washington law.
